volumes.title: Our First Number
volumes.text:
The Branch Line Gazette, January number, being the first. Edited by Mr. P. Nibley, booking clerk at Emberwick, and printed on the parcels office duplicator, which accounts for the purple. Our line is fourteen miles long and has six stations, from Lowland Junction to Grey Coast. Until today it had no newspaper. We mean to appear monthly and to report everything, there being about enough of it.

NOTICE. The Directors announce a silver cup for the Best Kept Station, to be judged in November by the District Inspector. Mr. Tulley, stationmaster at Emberwick, has already been seen measuring his flower bed with ticket string. Mrs. Reed of Marsh Halt says she has seen cups before.

LOST PROPERTY. Found on the 8.15: one umbrella, black, with a handle carved as a duck’s head. It may be claimed at the booking office. The duck looks patient.

volumes.title: A Question of Geraniums
volumes.text:
The Branch Line Gazette, February number. Edited by P. Nibley, booking clerk, Emberwick. Circulation last month: forty-one, counting the copy the goat ate at Withy Bridge.

THE CUP. With nine months until the Best Kept Station is judged, Mr. Tulley of Emberwick has ordered two hundred geraniums. He intends them to spell the station’s name in red along the bank. Mrs. Reed, porter-in-charge at Marsh Halt, has ordered nothing. She has, however, been seen carrying bean poles toward the signal post, and the signalman has asked us to print that he objects.

WEATHER. Snow on the Fellfoot bank on Tuesday. The 7.05 arrived wearing a white hat and eleven minutes late. LOST PROPERTY. The umbrella with the duck’s-head handle remains unclaimed. We have moved it to a hook by the stove, where the duck seems more comfortable.

volumes.title: Whitewash at Fellfoot Road
volumes.text:
The Branch Line Gazette, March number, from the booking office at Emberwick, where your editor Mr. Nibley sells tickets between paragraphs. LOST PROPERTY. One duck-headed umbrella, still. Also one glove, claimed within the hour by the owner of its fellow.

FELLFOOT ROAD ENTERS. Young Tam Ogle, the only porter at Fellfoot Road, has declared for the Best Kept Station cup. His method is whitewash. In one week he has whitened the platform edge, the coal bunker, the fence, forty-two stones and, by mistake, one side of a sheep that leaned. The sheep’s owner has been spoken to and is said to prefer it.

EMBERWICK. Mr. Tulley’s two hundred geraniums have arrived by goods train and are living in the waiting room until the frosts are over. Passengers are asked not to sit on the ones marked W.

volumes.title: Shells and a Lifebelt
volumes.text:
The Branch Line Gazette, April number. Edited at Emberwick by P. Nibley, booking clerk, with reports from all six stations of our fourteen miles.

FROM GREY COAST. Mr. Josiah Pinch, stationmaster at the seaside end, writes that flowers will not stand his wind, so he is competing for the Best Kept Station cup with shells. He has edged both platforms in cockles and hung a lifebelt, freshly painted, beside the clock. Gulls have removed some of the cockles. He regards this as the judge’s problem.

MARSH HALT. Mrs. Reed’s runner beans are up the signal post to the height of a tall child. The signalman reports that he can still see his signal arm, for now. LOST PROPERTY. We lent the duck-headed umbrella to a lady caught in Thursday’s shower. She returned it dry and said it was not hers either.

volumes.title: The Planting Out
volumes.text:
The Branch Line Gazette, May number. P. Nibley, editor and booking clerk, Emberwick.

A GREAT DAY. On Saturday Mr. Tulley planted out his geraniums on the bank opposite platform one. He used a plumb line, a yardstick and the station cat, who was not helpful. By the arrival of the 4.20 the bank read EMBERWICK in red letters three feet high. The driver sounded his whistle. Several passengers applauded from the windows, and one asked whether it was there to remind us.

LOST PROPERTY. The umbrella. Enquiries have now been made at every station on the line. The duck on the handle keeps its own counsel. A SMALL MATTER. Nothing whatever has been done at Withy Bridge, which has no staff, only a shelter, a lamp and the goat belonging to the mill. We mention it for completeness.

volumes.title: Ember Ick
volumes.text:
The Branch Line Gazette, June number, edited at the Emberwick booking office by Mr. P. Nibley, who saw the whole thing and could do nothing, having a queue.

DISASTER ON THE BANK. On Wednesday the Withy Bridge goat, travelling without a ticket in the guard’s van of the 10.30, alighted at Emberwick and ate the letter W. Mr. Tulley’s geraniums now spell EMBER ICK. The goat was returned by the next train. The W was not. Mr. Tulley has taken it quietly, which worries everyone. Mrs. Reed of Marsh Halt, his chief rival for the Best Kept Station cup, sent six spare geraniums up the line in a bucket, with a note that said only: For the gap.

LOST PROPERTY. One umbrella, duck-headed, five months. One goat, briefly.

volumes.title: Slugs and Diplomacy
volumes.text:
The Branch Line Gazette, July number. Edited by P. Nibley at Emberwick, where the bank once again says EMBERWICK, the W being slightly pinker than its neighbours.

MARSH HALT. Slugs have found Mrs. Reed’s runner beans. She patrols the signal post at dusk with a lantern and a jam jar. Mr. Tulley, remembering six geraniums in a bucket, sent down a sack of soot for the roots and a page of advice in copperplate. The two rivals for the cup were afterwards seen sharing a bench at the Junction, discussing greenfly. Each denies it.

WITHY BRIDGE. A passenger reports poppies along the platform fence. We assume the wind. LOST PROPERTY. The duck-headed umbrella has been dusted. A gentleman claimed it on Friday, looked the duck in the eye, and admitted that his had been a swan.

volumes.title: Water by the Bucket
volumes.text:
The Branch Line Gazette, August number, from your editor Mr. Nibley in the Emberwick booking office, with the window open and a wasp.

DROUGHT. No rain for twenty-six days. The water butts at Emberwick ran dry on the ninth, and Mr. Tulley’s geraniums began to hang their heads. Driver Enoch Pask now stops the engine Heron a yard short of her mark each evening and lets a little water from her tank into a row of buckets. This is against at least two rules. We have not seen it and nor have you.

LOST PROPERTY. Umbrella, duck-headed. Nobody wants an umbrella in August. ELSEWHERE. Fellfoot Road reports its whitewash has never looked whiter. Grey Coast reports sunburnt cockles. At Withy Bridge there are hollyhocks now, and a row of something like peas. The wind there is evidently tidy.

volumes.title: Beans for Everyone
volumes.text:
The Branch Line Gazette, September number. Edited by P. Nibley, booking clerk, Emberwick.

HARVEST. The runner beans on the signal post at Marsh Halt have reached the lamp. Mrs. Reed picked eleven pounds on Monday and sent a bundle up the line by every train, tied to the single-line token so that no signalman could refuse it. Your editor had his with butter. THE CUP. Two months to judging. Mr. Tulley has clipped his geraniums with nail scissors. Young Tam at Fellfoot Road has whitewashed the whitewash. Mr. Pinch at Grey Coast has replaced nineteen cockles and named the gull responsible.

LOST PROPERTY. The duck-headed umbrella enters its ninth month. We have begun saying good morning to it. A PUZZLE. Somebody has painted the Withy Bridge shelter green. The Company says it was not the Company.

volumes.title: The Gale
volumes.text:
The Branch Line Gazette, October number, edited at Emberwick by Mr. P. Nibley and delayed two days by weather.

THE GALE. On the night of the fourteenth a wind came in off the Grey Coast and went the length of our line. At Grey Coast, Mr. Pinch’s lifebelt was found in a field. At Fellfoot Road the fence lay down. At Marsh Halt the beans, poles and all, left the signal post and have not been seen since. At Emberwick the bank now reads, as nearly as we can make out, E B RW K. With the judging three weeks off, no staffed station on the line is fit to be seen. Mr. Tulley and Mrs. Reed spent Sunday on each other’s platforms with brooms.

LOST PROPERTY. The duck-headed umbrella was lent to the editor during the gale. It held. We think more of it than ever.

volumes.title: The Inspector’s Special
volumes.text:
The Branch Line Gazette, November number. P. Nibley, editor, Emberwick booking office.

JUDGING DAY. The District Inspector, Mr. Corbel, travelled the line on Tuesday in a saloon coach, judging the Best Kept Station. He found Grey Coast short of cockles, Fellfoot Road whitewashed over its damage, Marsh Halt swept bare, and Emberwick spelling its name in the few geraniums the gale had left, eked out with painted flowerpots. He was polite at each.

Then, at Withy Bridge, where trains stop only by request, he requested. He was on the platform nine minutes. Your editor, leaning from a window, saw a green shelter, a clipped hedge, late marigolds in a row, and the goat tethered well away from them. Mr. Corbel wrote for some time. LOST PROPERTY. The umbrella, as before. THE RESULT will appear next month.

volumes.title: The Cup and the Duck
volumes.text:
The Branch Line Gazette, December number, closing our first year. Edited by P. Nibley, booking clerk, Emberwick.

THE CUP for the Best Kept Station goes to Withy Bridge. The gardener has owned up: Mr. Garrow, the lengthman, who walks our fourteen miles of track each week and has planted that platform out of his coat pockets since spring. He accepted the cup in the Emberwick waiting room and asked if it would hold soup. Mr. Tulley and Mrs. Reed led the cheering, and have since exchanged cuttings.

LOST PROPERTY. On the twentieth a small lady in a grey hat asked for an umbrella with a duck’s-head handle. She left it on the 8.15 in January, she said, quite on purpose, her own hall being damp. She thanked us for the year’s storage. The hook by the stove looks bare. We resume in January.

volumes.title: Twelve Minutes Exactly
volumes.text:
My name is Ida Pettigrew, and I keep the refreshment room on platform one at Emberwick. I have two things on the wall behind my counter: a looking-glass, which I seldom consult, and the Company’s timetable, which I know as other people know their prayers.

Ours is a single line. Every train from the Junction must wait at Emberwick for the train from Grey Coast to pass it, and the timetable allows twelve minutes for the purpose. Twelve minutes is exactly long enough for a person to step down, drink one hot cup of tea, eat one currant bun and step up again without running.

I light the urn at six. She is copper, older than I am and slow to forgive, and I call her the Duchess. By the first whistle she is singing. That is my whole trade: a timetable, an urn and twelve minutes.

volumes.title: The 7.05 and Forty Cups
volumes.text:
The first train I serve at my refreshment room in Emberwick station is the 7.05 down, which carries the reed-cutters to the marsh sidings and the quarrymen on to Fellfoot Road. They come through my door all at once, forty men in a twelve-minute wait, and not one of them talkative at that hour.

So the cups stand ready in rows of ten, milk in first, sugar according to a chart I keep in my head. Mr. Hobb takes three lumps. The Dunn brothers take none and look pained at those who do. I pour down the rows with the big pot in one long stroke, like a woman watering beans, and Albie the junior porter carries two cans along to the driver and fireman.

At eleven minutes the guard looks in. At twelve the room is empty and warm, and smells of wet coats.

volumes.title: Buns for the 8.15
volumes.text:
The 8.15 up is the school train. I am Mrs. Pettigrew of the Emberwick refreshment room, and from September to July that train brings me eighteen children bound for the grammar school at the Junction, with twelve minutes to wait and a penny each.

A penny buys a currant bun, yesterday’s, split and buttered. I do not sell children tea. They get milk if they have been civil and water if they have not, and they know which they have been before I say so.

Cuthbert Lowe is late every morning of his life. I hear his boots on the footbridge as the guard lifts his flag. So his bun goes on the windowsill of the last compartment, in a paper bag, and a hand comes out and takes it as the train moves. I have never once had the penny late.

volumes.title: A Notice in Purple Ink
volumes.text:
In April a notice came to Emberwick station in a long envelope, and Mr. Tulley the stationmaster brought it across to my refreshment room, which told me it was bad before I had read a word.

It was from the Timetable Office at the Junction. From the first of June, in the interests of efficiency, the wait at Emberwick would be reduced from twelve minutes to four. It was signed L. Fenn, in purple ink, with a flourish under the name like a siding.

Four minutes. I worked it out. A cup of tea poured properly is too hot to drink for three. A person needs one to get down from the carriage and cross the platform. That leaves no minutes at all for the tea to be a pleasure, and none for the bun. I gave Mr. Tulley a cup anyway. He needed it.

volumes.title: The Four-Minute Experiment
volumes.text:
Before the new timetable came in, I tested it. I am Ida Pettigrew, I have kept the refreshment room at Emberwick station for nineteen years, and I do not condemn a thing untried.

Albie the porter played the passenger. Mr. Tulley held the station clock. On the first trial Albie reached my counter in fifty seconds, was served in twenty, and then stood blowing on his tea until Mr. Tulley called four minutes with the cup still full. On the second I poured beforehand, and he drank it in comfort, stone cold. On the third I gave him half a cup. He said it was like half a handshake. On the fourth he drank it hot regardless, and could taste nothing at dinner.

The Duchess, my urn, hissed through all of it. I took her meaning.

volumes.title: Letters to Mr. Fenn
volumes.text:
I wrote to the Timetable Office. I am no letter-writer; I keep the refreshment room on Emberwick station, and my hand is better suited to a teapot. But the wait at Emberwick was to be cut from twelve minutes to four, and somebody had to say what four minutes does to a cup of tea.

My first letter was polite. The answer was a printed card: Your communication has been received. My second enclosed the results of my experiments. Another card. With my third I sent a petition, signed by forty reed-cutters and quarrymen, eighteen schoolchildren, two drivers and a commercial traveller in buttons, all on the back of a bun bag because it was what we had.

That one was answered by hand. The purple ink said: Madam, trains are not run for the convenience of buns. L. Fenn. I pinned it over the counter, beside the timetable.

volumes.title: The First of June
volumes.text:
On the first of June the new timetable came into force, and the trains were given four minutes at Emberwick instead of twelve. I had the Duchess singing by six as usual, and the cups set out in their rows in my refreshment room on platform one. Habit is hard to argue with.

The 7.05 drew in. Nobody got down. Forty men looked at me through the carriage windows, and I looked at them over forty cups. Mr. Hobb raised his hand, the way you would to a neighbour across a river. Then the guard blew, four minutes to the tick, and they were gone toward the marsh with nothing hot inside them.

I poured the tea back into the pot, which you should never do, and sat down on the customers’ side of my own counter. It is a draughty side. I had not known.

volumes.title: The Runaway Trolley
volumes.text:
If passengers could no longer come to my tea, I decided, my tea would go to them. The new timetable allowed trains only four minutes at Emberwick, so Albie the porter and I fitted out a luggage barrow as a refreshment trolley: the second-best urn lashed on with parcel string, cups in a drawer from the lost property cupboard, buns under a cloth.

It answered well for two days. On the third the 11.40 stopped a carriage short, I pushed harder than I meant to, and the barrow found the ramp at the platform end. It went down by itself, steaming, at about the speed of a trotting pony, and came to rest in Mr. Tulley’s geraniums.

What vexed me most was this. The train from Grey Coast was late, as it very often is, and the 11.40 stood there nine full minutes with everybody afraid to get out.

volumes.title: A Man with a Stopwatch
volumes.text:
One wet morning in August a thin gentleman got down from the 9.50 at Emberwick, let it go without him, and stood on my platform with a stopwatch in one hand and a notebook in the other. He timed the porter. I believe he timed a pigeon. Then the rain came on harder, and he came into my refreshment room and asked what there was.

There was tea, I said, and seed cake cut that morning, and any amount of time to enjoy them in, since the Timetable Office had seen to it that I had no customers. I told him about the twelve minutes that had become four. I may have gone on. I showed him the note pinned over my counter.

He read it twice. Then he took out his own pen to write down the price of seed cake, and the ink was purple.

volumes.title: Mr. Fenn Misses His Train
volumes.text:
Mr. Lucius Fenn of the Timetable Office came to Emberwick three days running, and sat each day at the corner table of my refreshment room with his stopwatch beside his saucer. He had cut our wait from twelve minutes to four. He wished to know, he said, why his trains declined to keep to it.

So I told him what the old twelve minutes had been for. In them the engine took water. The single-line token changed hands. Parcels went in, hens came out, and the guard’s dog was walked to the lamp post. Forty men got warm. A railway, I said, wants somewhere to draw breath, and his timetable had it holding its nose.

He wrote all that down. He was on his second slice of seed cake, and still writing, when the 2.15 left without him. I did not point it out. The Duchess whistled a little.

volumes.title: Fourteen Minutes
volumes.text:
The winter timetable reached Emberwick in the last week of September. Mr. Tulley the stationmaster carried it across to my refreshment room at a trot, with his thumb marking the page.

Emberwick: arrive 7.05, depart 7.19. I counted on my fingers like a child. Fourteen minutes. Not the four we had suffered all summer, nor even the old twelve, but fourteen, at every train of the day. At the foot of the column stood a small printed teacup, and beside it the words: Refreshments obtainable.

On the first Monday the 7.05 drew in and every door opened at once. Forty men came across the platform. Mr. Hobb put down his penny and said, “Three lumps, Mrs. Pettigrew,” as if he had been gone one night and not four months. I poured down the rows in one stroke. My hand was not quite steady, and nobody mentioned it.

volumes.title: The 9.40 and Goodnight
volumes.text:
The last train I serve is the 9.40 down to Grey Coast. By then my refreshment room at Emberwick has only the one lamp lit, and the passengers are few: a nurse, a fiddler going home, sometimes a sailor asleep on his kitbag. They get what is left in the pot and the end of the seed cake, at half price.

Mr. Fenn of the Timetable Office travels by it on the first Friday of each month. He says he is observing the fourteen minutes he gave us. He observes them from the corner table, with cake. Last time he left a penny too much, and a timetable with my teacup inked over in purple.

When the tail lamp has gone round the curve I let the Duchess cool, rinse the last cup and turn the card in the door. Six o’clock comes early.

volumes.title: Three, Pause, One
volumes.text:
Nell Arkwright had been a signalwoman for eleven days when the fog came. It rose off the marsh after midnight and leaned on the windows of Marsh Halt signal box until she could not see her own home signal, forty yards off. She had the stove, the lamp, the levers in their painted row, and the two block bells that spoke to the boxes on either side.

Nothing was due until the milk train at ten to five. She made tea.

At ten past two the Emberwick bell rang. Three beats, a pause, one more. Nell knew her bell codes as she knew her own name; she had been examined in them only that month. This was not among them. She tapped a single beat back, which means I am here, speak. The bell stayed silent. Outside, the fog went on saying nothing at all.

volumes.title: Damp in the Wires
volumes.text:
In the morning Nell Arkwright, night signalwoman at Marsh Halt, told the day man what she had heard: an unknown bell signal out of the fog at ten past two, three beats, a pause and one.

Mr. Osric Bream had worked the box for sixteen years and did not care to be told things in it. Damp, he said. Fog got into the wires and the bells rang by themselves. He hung up his coat as though the matter hung there with it.

Nell had grown up beside this railway. A damp bell, she knew, gives a single dull clunk, or a stutter. It does not count three, wait, and add one, as neatly as a person laying a table. She wrote the time and the signal in the train register, in pencil, and drew a small square round the entry so that she could find it again.

volumes.title: Emberwick Heard It Too
volumes.text:
The fog held a second night over the marsh. Nell Arkwright sat in Marsh Halt signal box with the train register open at her pencilled note about a bell signal nobody could explain, and watched the clock climb toward two.

At ten past, the Emberwick bell rang: three, pause, one. She cranked the telephone to Emberwick box, two miles up the line, and Hale Dobbin answered with a yawn in his voice. “Was that you, Hale?” she asked. “Me? I was going to ask you,” he said. “My bell’s just gone the same. Three and a one. I’ve not touched my tapper since the last train.”

So the signal had rung at both ends of the section at once. Nell put the receiver back. Whoever sent it was not in her box, and not in Hale’s. They were somewhere in the two dark miles between.

volumes.title: The Lamp That Lit Itself
volumes.text:
At first light, with the fog thinning, Nell Arkwright walked down the line from Marsh Halt box to look at her distant signal. Wilf Tansy the lampman had confessed that he had forgotten to fill it two days ago. It ought to have burned dry in the night.

It was burning. She climbed the ladder. The lamp was full, the glass polished, and the wick had been trimmed straight across, square as a chisel. Wilf trimmed his wicks round, like a thumbnail; he had shown her on her first day and been proud of it.

On the bottom rung, in the frost, was half a boot print. The heel had an iron plate shaped like a horseshoe, worn right through on one side. Nell set her own boot beside it. Longer than hers, and narrow. She drew the heel in her notebook before the sun could take it.

volumes.title: A Paper of Peppermints
volumes.text:
Nell Arkwright, the new signalwoman at Marsh Halt, had two puzzles from two foggy nights: a bell signal that no rule book listed, and a signal lamp filled and trimmed by somebody who was not the lampman. On the third morning she found a third.

In fog, small warning caps are clipped to the rail beside the distant signal, so that a driver who cannot see is told by a crack under his wheels. That night she had had nobody to send. Yet there they sat on the rail, three of them, spaced as exactly as buttons on a waistcoat. In the lamp hut the tin was three short, with its lid put back straight. On the shelf lay a twist of paper holding two striped peppermints. The hut smelled of them, and faintly of pipe.

A thief who tidies, thought Nell, and who does my work for me.

volumes.title: The Old Code Book
volumes.text:
Mrs. Reed, who had charge of Marsh Halt station, held that the bell in the fog was the Grey Signalman, a ghost she had invented on the spot and grew fonder of hourly. Mr. Bream the day man still said damp. Nell Arkwright, who worked the box by night and had heard the thing ring three, pause, one, went looking for a third opinion in the stationmaster’s cupboard at Emberwick.

Behind the spare flags she found a bell code book with a brown cover, printed for the old Ember Valley Railway before the present Company bought it. She ran her finger down the column. Three, pause, one: Is line clear for goods train.

Inside the cover someone had stamped Withdrawn, and a date twenty-six years gone. Ghosts, she supposed, need not learn codes. Somebody had learned this one long ago, and never unlearned it.

volumes.title: The Second Hook
volumes.text:
Mr. Latchford the linesman came out to Marsh Halt to test the bell wires, because the night signalwoman, Nell Arkwright, kept reporting a signal that rang from nowhere on foggy nights. He found the wires sound. Then he remembered something.

Reed Siding box, a mile up toward Emberwick, had been shut three years ago when the reed-cutters’ siding was lifted. They took out the levers. They never took out the bell tapper. It was still in the circuit, to save a journey, and anyone pressing it would ring both neighbours at once.

The box was kept locked. Nell went to see its key, which hung in the stationmaster’s office at Emberwick, grey with dust. Beside it was a second hook, labelled Reed Siding, No. 2. That hook was empty. In the key book, No. 2 had been signed out long before Nell was born, and never signed in.

volumes.title: A Warm Stove
volumes.text:
Reed Siding signal box stood by itself in the reed beds, a mile from Marsh Halt, with its windows boarded and its name board gone. It had been shut three years. Nell Arkwright walked out to it along the track on her rest day, under a white sky, because a bell signal was coming from it on foggy nights and she meant to know whose finger was on the tapper.

The steps had been swept. The door was locked, but one board had a knot hole, and she put her eye to it. A stove, with its door ajar and grey ash inside. She laid her palm on the chimney pipe where it came through the wall. Barely warm; but warm.

On the shelf where the block bells used to stand were a tin mug, a kettle, and a train register lying open, with a pen across it.

volumes.title: Mrs. Reed Remembers
volumes.text:
Nobody knew the people of the marsh as Mrs. Reed did, so Nell Arkwright took her questions to the Marsh Halt booking office. Who had last worked Reed Siding box before it shut? Who would still have its second key, and know a bell code withdrawn twenty-six years ago, and trim a lamp wick square?

Mrs. Reed gave up her ghost with regret. “That’s Jethro Vane,” she said. “Forty-one years in that box. They retired him the day they shut it. He lives at Crossing Cottage with his daughter, and she says he’s never slept through a fog in his life. Stands at the window in his nightshirt.” “Does he eat peppermints?” asked Nell. “By the pound,” said Mrs. Reed. “And wears his father’s boots, heel plates and all.”

Nell closed her notebook. She had her answer on paper. She found she wanted it from the man himself.

volumes.title: The Watch at Reed Siding
volumes.text:
The fog came back on the Sunday. It was Nell Arkwright’s night off from Marsh Halt box. She put on two coats, filled a flask, and at one in the morning walked up the track to the shut signal box at Reed Siding, where she sat down on the bottom step to wait for whoever came there to ring the bell.

For an hour there was only dripping. Then a lantern showed along the path from Crossing Cottage, swinging low, and with it came the click of iron heel plates and a tune hummed round a peppermint.

An old man in a railway greatcoat climbed past her without seeing her, thin and very upright. A key turned. Above her head a stove door clanked, a match scraped, and, clear through the boards, a bell tapper went: three, pause, one. “Mr. Vane,” said Nell, from the stairs. “It’s line clear.”

volumes.title: Forty-One Winters
volumes.text:
Jethro Vane, three years retired, made tea for two in the closed signal box at Reed Siding and was not at all ashamed. Nell Arkwright, signalwoman at Marsh Halt, sat on the locker and listened while the fog pressed at the boards.

In his first winter, a goods train had stood lost in fog between two boxes for three hours, because each signalman thought the other had it. Nobody was hurt. The driver’s remarks were remembered for a generation. After that Jethro asked after the 2.05 goods every foggy night for forty-one years, and when they took off the goods train, and then shut the box, he found he could not stop asking.

He had thought the bell was dead. The lamp and the fog caps he saw to on his way, since Wilf forgot. His register held three years of fogs, each entered: On watch. All passed safe.

volumes.title: Fogman on Watch
volumes.text:
Nell Arkwright might have reported an intruder in the old signal box at Reed Siding. Instead she wrote four pages to the District Inspector, and Mr. Tulley, the stationmaster at Emberwick, read them twice and signed.

The answer came within the week. Mr. Jethro Vane was appointed fogman for the Marsh Halt section: called out in fog, paid by the night, and trusted with the lamps, the fog caps and the key he had never handed in. Mr. Bream said he had suspected as much. Mrs. Reed said the Grey Signalman would be missed.

The next fog came in December. Nell sat in her box with the stove ticking. At ten past two the bell rang: three, pause, one. She opened the local instructions, where a new line stood in her own handwriting. Fogman on watch. She tapped back one beat, I am here, and poured her tea.

series.name: The Last Train to Grey Coast

volumes.title: The 8.55, My Last
volumes.text:
Lowland Junction, platform three, Midwinter Eve. I am Ezra Coombe, guard, and this is the 8.55 to Grey Coast, the last train of the night. It is also my last train of any kind. Thirty-eight years on the Emberwick branch end when I hang up my lamp at the far end tonight, and I have told nobody on board, because I would rather do the job properly than be fussed over.

Two coaches and my van. The engine is Heron, with Enoch Pask driving. Eleven passengers, among them a cello with a man attached, a goose in a basket, a sailor already asleep, and a girl of eight named Posy Larkin with a label tied to her coat button: To Grey Coast. Please see she gets there.

The main line connection is seven minutes late. We wait for it. We always have. Then I show green, and we go.

volumes.title: Fog at Marsh Halt
volumes.text:
The 8.55 from the Junction, last train of the night to Grey Coast, runs out across the Lowlands in the dark with myself, Ezra Coombe, in the guard’s van. I have ridden this van thirty-eight years. Tonight is the last time, so I am noticing things: how the lamp swings, how the floor drums over the river Ember bridge and then goes quiet on the marsh, as if the train had taken its boots off.

Marsh Halt comes up out of fog. Mrs. Reed is on the platform with a lantern, and nobody gets on or off. She hands up the mailbag and then, without a word, a brick hot from her oven, wrapped in flannel, for my feet.

She has done that every winter night for twenty years. I say thank you as I always do, as if it were nothing much. The signal drops. We go on.

volumes.title: The Admiral at Large
volumes.text:
Between Marsh Halt and Emberwick the last train to Grey Coast has two miles of straight track and nothing to do, which is when things happen. I, Ezra Coombe, the guard, am checking parcels in my van when Mrs. Skerry’s basket, labelled Live Goose, This Way Up, turns out to be the wrong way up and open.

The goose is called the Admiral. He is not for eating; he is a present for her sister and has, she says, opinions. He walks the length of the first coach like an inspector. He looks at the sleeping sailor and at the cello. He stops by Posy Larkin, a girl travelling alone, who has been sitting up straight and not crying, and puts his head in her lap.

I leave him there. The Company’s rules on geese are clear. I have obeyed rules for thirty-eight years and have about an hour left.

volumes.title: Fourteen Minutes at Emberwick
volumes.text:
Emberwick, 9.33, seven minutes down. I am Ezra Coombe, guard of the last train to Grey Coast, and the timetable gives us fourteen minutes here, which tonight nobody wastes.

One lamp is lit in the refreshment room. Mrs. Pettigrew gives the cellist tea, wakes nobody, and sends a cup of warm milk out to the girl with the label on her coat, who drinks it at the carriage door with a goose looking on. Enoch Pask takes water for the engine. Mr. Tulley the stationmaster walks the platform with me, trying doors I have already tried.

At the van he shakes my hand a moment longer than usual. So he knows it is my last trip. Stationmasters hear everything. He says only, “Snow on the Fells, Ezra. Mind the bank.” Then he steps back, and Mrs. Pettigrew turns down her lamp, and I blow.

volumes.title: A Lamp at Withy Bridge
volumes.text:
Withy Bridge is a request stop: a shelter, a lamp and a goat. In thirty-eight years as guard on this line I, Ezra Coombe, have seen the last train to Grey Coast stop there perhaps a dozen times. Tonight somebody is swinging a lamp on the platform, and Enoch brings the engine to a stand.

It is old Mr. Garrow the lengthman, with a sack for a cape. He does not want to travel. He has a parcel, warm, tied in a cloth: a mutton pie for his sister at Grey Coast, who has had one from him every Midwinter Eve since they were young. He missed the afternoon train on account of the goat.

He has no label and no money. I take the pie into the van and write the ticket myself. The first flakes of snow come down through the lamplight as we pull away.

volumes.title: The Fellfoot Bank
volumes.text:
After Withy Bridge the line climbs for two miles to Fellfoot Road, and tonight the last train to Grey Coast has snow on the rails. I am Ezra Coombe, the guard. From my van I can hear Heron working: a slow, heavy beat, then a sudden flurry as her wheels slip, then the beat again.

Halfway up she stops. It is not dangerous, only still. The snow comes past the windows quite silently. Enoch Pask is out with the sand bucket and his fireman with a shovel, and I walk through the two coaches to tell eleven passengers that we shall be a little while and are in no difficulty.

Nobody complains. Mrs. Skerry shares out gingerbread. The girl Posy asks whether trains get tired. I tell her yes, on hills, like anybody, and that this one has never yet failed to reach the top.

volumes.title: Music in the First Coach
volumes.text:
We are standing on the Fellfoot bank in the snow, the last train of the night to Grey Coast, while the engine crew sand the rails ahead. I am the guard, Ezra Coombe, and I have nothing to do but keep eleven people cheerful.

Mr. Dando does it for me. He takes the cello out of its case, wedges himself across two seats, and plays. It is no tune I know: something slow and brown, like a river in autumn, and then a jig that sets the lamp glasses buzzing. The sailor sleeps through it, smiling. The Admiral, a goose, joins in once and is hushed. Posy Larkin keeps time on the label tied to her coat.

Partway through the jig I feel the couplings tighten. Heron has found her feet. We move off uphill at a walking pace, with music going out of the windows into the dark.

volumes.title: Wake Me at Fellfoot
volumes.text:
Fellfoot Road, the highest station on the branch, under two inches of snow. I am Ezra Coombe, guard of the last train to Grey Coast, now twenty-six minutes late, and I have a sailor to deliver.

He has slept since the Junction with his head on his kitbag and a card pinned to his jersey: Wake me at Fellfoot Road. I shake his shoulder. He comes up all at once, asking whose watch it is. I tell him it is his mother’s.

She is on the platform under the one lamp, a small woman in a man’s coat, with Tam the porter holding a lantern beside her. She has met this train three nights running in case his ship was early. The sailor gets down. Neither of them says anything I can hear. He drops the kitbag and picks her up, and Tam looks tactfully at the snow.

volumes.title: Sheep in the Cutting
volumes.text:
Beyond Fellfoot Road the line runs through Gorse Cutting before it drops to the sea. Tonight, with the last train to Grey Coast nearly half an hour late, the cutting is full of sheep. They have come down off the Fells out of the snow, forty or so, and they stand between the rails in the light of the engine lamps looking put out.

I am the guard, Ezra Coombe, and the rule book makes livestock on the line my business. I go forward with my hand lamp. The fireman comes with his shovel. Mr. Dando comes too, uninvited, carrying his cello bow like a crook, and Mrs. Skerry’s goose sends his opinion from a window.

It takes twelve minutes. The last ewe goes up the bank with a look over her shoulder. I count them out of habit and walk back along the train in my own footprints.

volumes.title: Down to the Sea
volumes.text:
From Gorse Cutting it is downhill all the way. The last train to Grey Coast runs out from under the snow cloud, and from my van I, Ezra Coombe, guard, watch the sky clear from the seaward side, one star and then a great many.

This is the stretch I shall miss. The engine hardly works; she only holds us back, and the wheels make a long easy sound like something being poured. First you smell the sea, coal smoke and salt together. Then the line swings left round Cockle Point, and there is the harbour light, turning.

In the first coach Posy Larkin has her nose against the glass. I tell her the red lamp below the lighthouse is the station, and that somebody is standing under it. I cannot see that from here. But I have brought this train in for thirty-eight years, and somebody always is.

volumes.title: Grey Coast, Forty-One Late
volumes.text:
Grey Coast station, end of the line, 11.02 by the platform clock. The last train is forty-one minutes late, and every person who meant to meet it has waited. I am Ezra Coombe, the guard, and I open the doors myself.

Mrs. Skerry’s sister receives the Admiral and is hissed at fondly. Mr. Dando carries his cello off toward the harbour, where there is a dance he was to have started. A stout woman with a lantern takes a mutton pie from my hands, sniffs it, and says her brother has overdone the pepper again, which means it is right.

Last comes Posy Larkin, with her label. A tall old lady in a blue shawl reads it aloud, To Grey Coast, please see she gets there, and looks at me. “She got there,” I say. Posy takes her grandmother’s hand, and then, quickly, shakes mine.

volumes.title: Lamp Out
volumes.text:
When the last train has emptied at Grey Coast there is still the guard’s work to do, and tonight I, Ezra Coombe, do it slowly. I walk both coaches. I find a goose feather, gingerbread crumbs and one small red mitten, which I leave on the office door handle for a girl of eight to claim tomorrow.

Enoch Pask has uncoupled Heron and is taking her to the shed. He sounds the whistle as he passes my van, one long and two short, which is in no rule book. Mr. Pinch the stationmaster is waiting at the office door with the journal and a teapot and two cups.

I write it up. The 8.55 from the Junction, arrived 11.02, forty-one minutes late owing to snow and sheep. Eleven passengers. All delivered. Then I sign my name, turn down the wick, and hang the lamp on its hook.
